notes.subject: Fundamentals of Nursing
notes.definition: Arterial Blood Gas analysis measures blood pH, oxygenation, and carbon dioxide levels to evaluate acid-base balance.
keyPoints: pH Normal: 7.35 - 7.45
PaCO2 Normal (Respiratory): 35 - 45 mmHg
HCO3 Normal (Metabolic): 22 - 26 mEq/L
clinicalFeatures: Respiratory Acidosis: COPD, hypoventilation, CNS depression.
Metabolic Acidosis: DKA, severe diarrhea, renal failure.
Metabolic Alkalosis: Severe vomiting, prolonged NG suctioning.
diagnosis: Use ROME acronym: Respiratory Opposite, Metabolic Equal.
If pH and PaCO2 go in opposite directions = Respiratory.
If pH and HCO3 go in the same direction = Metabolic.
management: Metabolic Acidosis: Administer sodium bicarbonate IV, treat DKA with insulin.
nursingPoints: Perform Allen's Test before drawing ABG from the radial artery to confirm ulnar collateral circulation.
Place ABG specimen on ice immediately and transport to lab.
Apply firm pressure to the puncture site for at least 5 minutes (longer if on anticoagulants).
rapidRevision: Allen's test MUST be positive before radial puncture.

notes.subject: Fundamentals of Nursing
notes.definition: The IV administration of whole blood or its components for severe anemia, hemorrhage, or coagulation factor deficiencies.
keyPoints: Universal Donor: O Negative.
Universal Recipient: AB Positive.
Blood must be infused within 4 hours to prevent bacterial growth.
clinicalFeatures: Hemolytic Reaction: Back pain, hematuria, hypotension, tachycardia.
diagnosis: Two RNs must verify the patient and blood product at the bedside.
management: If ANY reaction occurs: 1) STOP the transfusion. 2) Maintain IV line with NORMAL SALINE using new tubing. 3) Notify MD. 4) Send blood bag and tubing to blood bank.
nursingPoints: Use ONLY 0.9% Normal Saline (NS) to flush or hang with blood.
Stay with the patient for the first 15 minutes of the transfusion.
Use an 18-gauge or 20-gauge IV catheter.
examTricks: Dextrose causes RBC hemolysis; Lactated Ringer's causes clotting (calcium). ALWAYS use NS.
First action for any reaction is to STOP the infusion.
rapidRevision: Start within 30 mins from lab, finish within 4 hours.

notes.subject: Fundamentals of Nursing
notes.definition: Basic Life Support guidelines by the American Heart Association (AHA) focusing on high-quality chest compressions and early defibrillation.
keyPoints: Compression to Ventilation ratio: 30:2 for adults.
Rate: 100-120 compressions per minute.
Depth: At least 2 inches (5 cm) but no more than 2.4 inches (6 cm) for adults.
clinicalFeatures: Unresponsiveness, absence of normal breathing, and no palpable pulse within 10 seconds.
management: Allow complete chest recoil after each compression.
Minimize interruptions to chest compressions to < 10 seconds.
nursingPoints: If an advanced airway (Intubation) is in place, give 1 breath every 6 seconds (10 breaths/min) without pausing compressions.
Switch compressors every 2 minutes or 5 cycles to prevent fatigue.
examTricks: Pulse check should take no more than 10 seconds.
For 2-rescuer Infant CPR, the ratio changes to 15:2.

notes.subject: Medical-Surgical Nursing
notes.definition: Irreversible necrosis of heart muscle secondary to prolonged ischemia (blockage of coronary arteries).
keyPoints: Chest pain is crushing, radiates to left arm/jaw, and is NOT relieved by rest or nitroglycerin.
Troponin I and T are the most specific biomarkers.
clinicalFeatures: Women/diabetics may present with atypical symptoms (fatigue, epigastric pain).
diagnosis: 12-Lead ECG: Look for ST elevation (STEMI), T-wave inversion.
Cardiac markers: Troponin rises within 3-4 hours, peaks at 24 hours.
management: MONA protocol: Morphine, Oxygen, Nitroglycerin, Aspirin.
Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI) is gold standard (Door-to-balloon < 90 mins).
nursingPoints: Ensure oxygen is applied FIRST if O2 sat < 90%.
Morphine decreases pain AND reduces preload/afterload.
Monitor continuously for ventricular arrhythmias (V-Fib is most common cause of early death).
examTricks: Nitroglycerin can be given every 5 mins x 3 doses. Call EMS if pain persists after 1st dose.
Myoglobin is the earliest marker but NOT specific. Troponin is highly specific.

notes.subject: Medical-Surgical Nursing
notes.definition: A rise in pressure within the skull (Normal ICP: 5 to 15 mmHg). Life-threatening due to brain herniation risk.
keyPoints: Monro-Kellie hypothesis: Brain, blood, and CSF volumes must remain constant.
Cushing's Triad is a LATE sign indicating impending herniation.
clinicalFeatures: Earliest sign: Altered Level of Consciousness (ALOC).
Late (Cushing's Triad): Systolic hypertension (widening pulse pressure), Bradycardia, Irregular respirations.
diagnosis: CT Scan / MRI of the brain.
management: Osmotic diuretic: Mannitol IV (monitor serum osmolality).
Hyperventilation (maintain PaCO2 between 30-35 mmHg to cause vasoconstriction).
nursingPoints: Elevate Head of Bed (HOB) to 30 degrees to promote venous drainage.
Keep head and neck strictly in neutral midline position.
Avoid clustering nursing activities; avoid coughing, straining, or Valsalva.
examTricks: Earliest sign of ICP = Restlessness/ALOC. Do NOT wait for Cushing's Triad.
Lumbar Puncture is CONTRAINDICATED in increased ICP (risk of brainstem herniation).

notes.subject: Pharmacology
notes.definition: Lifesaving medications used in critical care and resuscitation (ACLS/BLS).
keyPoints: Adrenaline (Epinephrine): 1mg IV every 3-5 mins in cardiac arrest.
Atropine: 1mg IV for symptomatic bradycardia (Max dose 3mg).
Amiodarone: 300mg IV push for VF/pVT, followed by 150mg.
Adenosine: 6mg rapid IV push for SVT, flush with 20mL NS.
clinicalFeatures: Cardiac Arrest: VF, pVT, Asystole, PEA.
Bradycardia: HR < 50/min with hypotension or altered mental status.
management: Flush line immediately after IV push (especially Adenosine).
Elevate extremity to facilitate central drug delivery.
nursingPoints: Adrenaline can cause severe tissue necrosis if extravasated.
Atropine is ineffective for complete heart block.
Adenosine half-life is < 10 seconds; requires rapid push.
examTricks: Drug of choice for anaphylaxis: IM Adrenaline (1:1000).
Drug of choice for cardiac arrest: IV Adrenaline (1:10000).

notes.subject: Pharmacology
notes.definition: Drugs bearing a heightened risk of causing significant patient harm when used in error (e.g., Insulin, Heparin).
keyPoints: Insulin: Only regular insulin can be given IV.
Heparin: Monitor aPTT (Normal: 30-40s, Therapeutic: 1.5-2.5x normal).
Warfarin: Monitor PT/INR (Normal INR: 1, Therapeutic: 2-3).
management: Insulin Hypoglycemia: 50% Dextrose IV or oral fast-acting carbs.
nursingPoints: Two RNs must independently verify Insulin and Heparin doses.
Never mix long-acting insulin (Glargine) with any other insulin.
Inject subcutaneous heparin in the abdomen, 2 inches away from umbilicus.
examTricks: Heparin = aPTT (10 letters), Warfarin = PT (10 letters).

notes.subject: Pharmacology
notes.definition: A potentially fatal condition resulting from toxic levels of the cardiac glycoside Digoxin (Therapeutic range: 0.5 - 2.0 ng/mL).
keyPoints: Digoxin acts by increasing myocardial contractility (+ inotrope) and decreasing heart rate (- chronotrope).
Hypokalemia drastically increases the risk of Digoxin toxicity.
Toxicity occurs when levels > 2.0 ng/mL.
clinicalFeatures: Late: Yellow-green halos around lights, blurred vision.
diagnosis: Serum Potassium levels (Hypokalemia is a trigger).
management: Hold the dose if apical pulse < 60 bpm in adults (< 90 in infants).
nursingPoints: Assess apical pulse for 1 full minute before administration.
Educate patient to consume potassium-rich foods if on loop diuretics.
Toxicity is NOT caused by hyperkalemia, it is CAUSED by hypokalemia.
examTricks: Earliest sign of toxicity = GI symptoms (Nausea/Vomiting).
Most specific visual sign = Yellow-green halos.
